title: The Reef Under the Ridge
subtitle: The Main Reef, the founding of Johannesburg and the first deep mines, Witwatersrand, South African Republic, 1884–1891
intro: In February 1886 two itinerant workmen building cottages on the farm Langlaagte, on the long quartzite ridge the Boers called the Witwatersrand, picked up a piece of conglomerate rock and crushed and panned it. What they found was not a vein but the outcrop of a reef that ran for miles and went down for thousands of feet: the richest goldfield ever found. Within seven months President Paul Kruger's South African Republic (ZAR) had proclaimed public diggings; within ten, a triangle of leftover government land called Randjeslaagte had been surveyed into stands and auctioned as Johannesburg.

The record here is mostly not diaries. It is affidavits sworn by prospectors, government proclamations and departmental letters, company letters, newspaper files, Chamber of Mines reports, and memoirs written much later by men who were there. The question of who found the reef first was argued for fifty-five years: George Harrison made sworn statements in 1886 and was granted the discoverer's claim, while George Walker and George Honeyball told different stories decades afterwards. Those are set out here as positions, with their dates, and no verdict.

The money came fast. J. B. Robinson arrived in July 1886 with a cheque from Alfred Beit; Cecil Rhodes and Charles Rudd bought more cautiously and founded the Gold Fields of South Africa in London in February 1887; Hermann Eckstein's firm at the Corner House became the centre of the Wernher-Beit interest. Then, in 1889, the oxidised ore near the surface gave way at depth to pyritic 'blue' rock from which mercury amalgamation recovered too little gold, and the share boom collapsed. The MacArthur-Forrest cyanide process, tried at the Salisbury mine in mid-1890, rescued the field and opened the way to deep-level mining.

The men who did the digging were overwhelmingly African migrants, many from Portuguese Mozambique, working on contracts, under pass regulations and the Master and Servant law, for wages the mine owners combined to push down. The Chamber of Mines, founded in 1887 and reconstituted in 1889, recorded them as a labour supply. No surviving firsthand account by an African mineworker on the Rand for 1886–1891 has been found for this chapter; what they earned, where they came from and how they were controlled is known from the owners' own reports, and those reports are used here plainly for what they show. The same holds for the Indian traders whom the ZAR's Law 3 of 1885 barred from burgher rights and from owning land outside assigned locations, and for the Chinese storekeepers of early Johannesburg: their petitions survive in collections such as Bhana and Pachai's Documentary History, but no diary of theirs is used here.

Between the burghers of the old republic and the uitlanders, the foreigners who outnumbered them in the new town, lay the quarrel that ran on to the Jameson Raid of December 1895. Kruger's memoirs, dictated in exile and published in English in 1902, give his side; Lord Randolph Churchill's letters of 1891 give a hostile English visitor's. Read together with the prospectors' affidavits and the Chamber's labour figures, they show the same reef as a find, a title deed, a share certificate, a state's salvation and a workplace.
calendar_note: All dates are Gregorian; the South African Republic used the Gregorian calendar. Several founding dates are disputed because the government issued a sequence of proclamations for different farms: Kruger signed the first on 8 September 1886, Driefontein and Elandsfontein were proclaimed from 20 September, and Randjeslaagte and Langlaagte on 4 October, the date Johannesburg now treats as its birthday. Memoirs written decades later (Walker 1924, Struben 1920, Sauer 1937) are placed at the dates of the events they describe, flagged as later accounts.

eyes.name: George Harrison
eyes.role: Itinerant prospector and builder, by his own statement an experienced Australian gold digger
eyes.where: Langlaagte farm, then Pretoria; vanished from the record late 1886
eyes.authenticity: Two statements to the ZAR Mines Department survive in the Transvaal archives: one dated 24 July 1886 and one dated 12 October 1886. Their wording is quoted in Johannesburg heritage publications. Almost nothing else is known of him.
eyes.bio: Harrison is the man the republic recognised: his sworn statement that the Langlaagte reef was payable helped trigger the proclamation, and he was granted the Discoverer's Claim (Langlaagte No. 19). He is said to have sold it for £10 and left the Rand within weeks. Whether he or his companion Walker first recognised the reef was argued long after he was gone.

sources.title: City of Johannesburg, 'Three Georges strike paydirt'
Mining Weekly, 'Just who discovered the Wits Main Reef Series?' (2016)

eyes.name: George Walker
eyes.role: Miner from Wigan, Lancashire, working as a builder and labourer for the Strubens and the Oosthuizens
eyes.authenticity: His account was given to the Sunday Times (6 April 1924) when he was 71, about 38 years after the events; later writers (Rosenthal 1970) retold it. In 1886 he signed documents acknowledging Harrison as discoverer, and was given an ordinary claim (Langlaagte No. 21).
eyes.bio: Walker spent his last decades insisting that he, not Harrison, had found the outcrop. He lived on a small allowance from the Chamber of Mines and died poor in Krugersdorp. His story is the later of the two and the more vivid; it is set beside Harrison's sworn statements as a position.

sources.title: Wigan Local History, 'George Walker of Wigan'
Mining Weekly (2016)

eyes.name: George Honeyball
eyes.role: Prospector and companion of Walker and Harrison
eyes.vantage_label: third man at the find (later recollection)
eyes.authenticity: His recollection, giving the day as Sunday 7 February 1886, is known through later Johannesburg histories; the date and place of its first publication have not been confirmed here.
eyes.bio: The third George. His memory fixes the find to a specific Sunday and adds that he himself found a second outcrop the next day, a detail that neither Harrison's statements nor Walker's account contains.

sources.title: City of Johannesburg, 'Three Georges strike paydirt'

eyes.name: Frederick Pine Theophilus Struben
eyes.role: Prospector; with his brother Harry the first to work gold on the central Rand
eyes.side: Natal-born English settlers in the ZAR
eyes.where: Wilgespruit farm, north of present Roodepoort
eyes.authenticity: Letters of 1885 are quoted in Mining Weekly's history series; his work is also described in Harry Struben's Recollections (1920).
eyes.bio: Fred Struben found and named the Confidence Reef in 1884, a rich but short-lived quartz reef a few miles west of the later Main Reef. The brothers' battery and the work it offered brought Walker and Harrison onto the Rand.

sources.title: Mining Weekly, 'The Confidence of the Wits basin'
Mining Weekly, 'Rand goldfield: Not worth hell room'

eyes.name: Hendrik Wilhelm (Harry) Struben
eyes.role: Prospector and promoter, elder of the Struben brothers
eyes.side: Natal-born English settlers in the ZAR
eyes.vantage_label: earlier finder, petitioner to the Volksraad
eyes.authenticity: Recollections of Adventures: Pioneering and Development in South Africa, 1850–1911, published posthumously in Cape Town in 1920, revised and edited by his daughter Edith.
eyes.bio: Harry Struben argued the brothers' case before the Volksraad in 1885 and won government support for the Confidence Reef. His memoir claims for the Strubens the opening of the Rand, a claim later commemorated by a monument that no longer stands.

sources.title: Harry Struben (Wikipedia)
Mining Weekly (2016)

eyes.name: Stephanus Johannes Paulus (Paul) Kruger
eyes.role: President of the South African Republic (1883–1900)
eyes.vantage_label: head of state who proclaimed the field
eyes.authenticity: The Memoirs of Paul Kruger, told by himself, dictated in exile and translated by A. Teixeira de Mattos (London, 1902). Written after the war and partisan; read here as his position. The 1886 proclamations survive in the Staatscourant and the Transvaal archives.
eyes.bio: Kruger saw the gold as both the republic's rescue from bankruptcy and a danger to its independence. His memoirs record his visits to the new town, the complaints he was handed, and his conviction that the franchise quarrel was exploited by outsiders. He also records General Joubert's warning that the gold would soak the country in blood.

sources.title: The Memoirs of Paul Kruger (1902), HathiTrust record
Memoirs, ch. 9 'On my first presidency' (text at Politicsweb)
Memoirs, ch. 10 'On my second presidency' (SAHO PDF)

eyes.name: Carl Friedrich Wilhelm von Brandis
eyes.role: Mining Commissioner of the Witwatersrand goldfield from 1886; former soldier from Hanover
eyes.authenticity: His official correspondence was filed with the State Secretary in Pretoria. His letter of 3 October 1886 (No. 4996/86) is missing from the archive; it survives only as a facsimile in E. L. and J. Gray's history.
eyes.bio: Von Brandis read the proclamation to the diggers, administered the claims and stands, and wrote the earliest surviving official reference to the name of the new town. A riot in front of his house in March 1890, during Kruger's visit, ended with the republic's flag torn down.

sources.title: Heritage Portal, 'Naming Johannesburg'
City of Johannesburg, 'Three Georges strike paydirt'

eyes.name: Johann Friedrich Bernhard Rissik
eyes.role: Surveyor in the Surveyor-General's office, ZAR
eyes.authenticity: The report of Rissik and Mines Minister C. J. Joubert is dated 12 August 1886. His departmental note of 9 September 1896 on the town's name was quoted by M. S. Appelgryn in 1971; it is the only written statement on the name from anyone involved.
eyes.bio: Rissik and Joubert were sent to inspect the reef before proclamation and chose the triangle of unclaimed government land for the town. Ten years later Rissik wrote that the town had been named for the two of them, a statement the city council accepted in 1975.

sources.title: Heritage Portal, 'Naming Johannesburg'
Heritage Portal, 'Johannesburg goldfield discovered'

eyes.name: Hans Sauer
eyes.role: Free State-born doctor and lawyer; agent buying claims for Rhodes and Rudd; Johannesburg's first district surgeon
eyes.authenticity: Ex Africa (London: G. Bles, 1937), written half a century after the events; vivid but self-flattering and undated in places. Extracts are quoted by Meredith and Mining Weekly.
eyes.bio: Sauer rode to the Rand in the same coach as J. B. Robinson, watched Robinson buy while Rhodes hesitated, and bought for Rhodes on a 15 per cent share. His memoir preserves the American engineer Gardner Williams's dismissive verdict on the reef and Rhodes's abrupt departure in October 1886.

sources.title: Hans Sauer (Wikipedia)
Mining Weekly, 'Rand goldfield: Not worth hell room'
Meredith, Diamonds, Gold and War, ch. 18 (extract)

eyes.name: Charles Dunell Rudd
eyes.role: Rhodes's partner; co-founder of the Gold Fields of South Africa
eyes.authenticity: Letters to Alfred Curry and others in the Gold Fields and Rhodes papers, cited by I. R. Phimister; quoted here only in short phrases from his citations.
eyes.bio: Rudd and Rhodes came late and bought cautiously, then floated Gold Fields in London. By 1888–1892 Rudd's letters show the company's eyes turning north to Lobengula's country and Mashonaland, before the deep-level Rand pulled it back.

sources.title: I. R. Phimister, 'Rhodes, Rhodesia and the Rand'

eyes.name: The Eastern Star / The Star (Thomas and George Sheffield, proprietors)
eyes.role: Newspaper moved from Grahamstown to Johannesburg by the Sheffield brothers
eyes.authenticity: Founded in Grahamstown on 6 January 1871; first Johannesburg issue 17 October 1887; renamed The Star in 1889. Files survive in South African libraries. The proprietors are named as the eye; individual reporters are unidentified.
eyes.bio: The Star became the voice of the mining town and, increasingly, of the uitlander grievance. Its files record the stock markets, the slump and the labour regulations that the Chamber drafted.

sources.title: SAHO, 'The Star is published in Johannesburg'

eyes.name: Hermann Eckstein (president), for the Witwatersrand Chamber of Mines
eyes.role: Head of H. Eckstein & Co. at the Corner House and first president of the reconstituted Chamber of Mines (1889–1892)
eyes.authenticity: Witwatersrand Chamber of Mines Annual Reports from 1889; figures cited here from the 1890 report as analysed by Norman Levy. The reports are the owners' own record and present labour as a supply problem.
eyes.bio: The annual reports are the main source for how many African men worked the mines, where they came from and what they were paid. In 1890 the Chamber asked the state to hand over the native pass office to its own control and recorded a combined agreement to cut African wages.

sources.title: N. Levy, 'The state, mineowners and labour regulation in the Transvaal, 1887–1906'
Hermann Eckstein (Wikipedia)

eyes.name: Lionel Phillips
eyes.role: Mining financier from Kimberley; consultant then partner at H. Eckstein & Co. from 1889; Chamber president from 1892
eyes.side: Mine owners (Corner House); later Reform Committee
eyes.authenticity: Letters from 1890 onward edited by Maryna Fraser and Alan Jeeves as All That Glittered: Selected Correspondence of Lionel Phillips, 1890–1924 (1977); memoir Some Reminiscences (1924). The letters have not been consulted directly for this chapter; entries are kept to dated public facts.
eyes.bio: Phillips came to Johannesburg in the slump year and stayed to run the Corner House. After the Jameson Raid he was sentenced to death as a Reform Committee leader, reprieved and fined. His wife Florence later founded the Johannesburg Art Gallery.

sources.title: Lionel Phillips (Wikipedia)
All That Glittered (Business Archives Council record)

eyes.name: Lord Randolph Churchill
eyes.role: Conservative politician, former Chancellor of the Exchequer, travelling as correspondent for The Daily Graphic and head of a mining syndicate
eyes.authenticity: Letters to The Daily Graphic, collected as Men, Mines and Animals in South Africa (1892; new edition 1895). Private letters to Lady Randolph are in the Churchill Archives Centre, Cambridge.
eyes.bio: Churchill came to make money and wrote for the London public. He admired the mines, despised the Boer government and recorded what the mine managers told him: output, wages, the numbers of white and African workers, and the new chemistry. Five years before the Raid, his letters already rehearse the uitlander case.

sources.title: Men, Mines and Animals in South Africa (1895 ed., full text)
Biodiversity Heritage Library record
Churchill Archives Centre: letter of 17 June 1891

entries.headline: A promising quartz reef, and a name for it
entries.digest: After a month examining the ridge on Wilgespruit, Fred Struben struck a quartz reef showing visible gold and named it the Confidence Reef. Over the next six months the brothers sank shafts and sent samples for assay. It was a true vein, not the conglomerate that would make the Rand, and it would pinch out within a year.
entries.source_note: Mining Weekly, 'The Confidence of the Wits basin' (2016); SAHO Johannesburg timeline gives September 1884.

entries.headline: The Strubens put their gold before the Volksraad
entries.digest: Required to make their case in person, the Strubens appeared before the republic's parliament with their ore and results to support their application for a concession. Kruger thanked the brothers from the chair. The republic, nearly bankrupt, was eager for any field that might pay.
entries.source_note: Mining Weekly (2016), citing the account in Die Volkstem; concession applied for in March 1885.

entries.headline: Waiting on an American engineer's opinion
entries.digest: Fred Struben wrote that the judgement of Gardner Williams, the American mining engineer then managing a company at Pilgrim's Rest, was worth more than all the others' put together. The brothers needed outside credit for their reef. Williams would later become Rhodes's adviser and the Rand's sternest early sceptic.
entries.quote: worth more than the whole lot put together
entries.source_note: Letter of 22 July 1885 quoted in Mining Weekly, 'Rand goldfield: Not worth hell room' (2016).

entries.headline: A stamp battery on the ridge
entries.digest: With the concession granted, the brothers erected a stamp battery on Wilgespruit, the first on the central Rand. Its building drew labourers and tradesmen, among them two men heading for the Barberton diggings, George Walker and George Harrison.
entries.source_note: Mining Weekly (2016); Struben, Recollections (1920).

entries.headline: Gold in a frying pan
entries.digest: In Walker's telling, given 38 years later, he was walking on Willem Oosthuizen's portion of Langlaagte when he noticed an outcrop, broke off rock, crushed it and panned it in a frying pan borrowed from Mrs Oosthuizen. There was a tail of gold. He says he then secured a three-month option on the ground.
entries.source_note: Sunday Times, 6 April 1924, as summarised in Mining Weekly (2016); a later account, not a contemporary record.

entries.headline: A Sunday rock sample at the widow's house
entries.digest: Honeyball remembered the morning precisely: Walker came to the Oosthuizen house with a piece of rock from his outcrop. Harrison was then building a cottage for the widow Petronella Oosthuizen. The date rests on Honeyball's later memory alone.
entries.source_note: Honeyball's recollection as given in City of Johannesburg, 'Three Georges strike paydirt'.

entries.headline: A second outcrop six hundred metres off
entries.digest: The next day, by his account, Honeyball found a similar conglomerate outcrop some 600 metres from Walker's spot. If true, it showed the reef was a continuous bed and not a pocket. Neither Harrison's affidavits nor Walker's account mention it.
entries.source_note: City of Johannesburg, 'Three Georges strike paydirt'.

entries.headline: A written right to prospect
entries.digest: Harrison and Walker signed a contract with the farmer Gerhardus Cornelius Oosthuizen giving them prospecting rights on his portion of Langlaagte. Harrison then went to Pretoria for a one-month prospecting licence. Oosthuizen wrote separately to Kruger, in an undated letter, that the reef was payable.
entries.source_note: SAHO Johannesburg timeline (12 April 1886); City of Johannesburg, 'Three Georges strike paydirt'.

entries.place: Coach from Kimberley to the Rand
entries.headline: Riding north beside Robinson and Beit's cheque
entries.digest: Sauer shared the coach to the Rand with J. B. Robinson, who carried a £20,000 cheque from Alfred Beit for a third share in his syndicate. In late July Robinson made an offer on part of Langlaagte one day and bought another part outright the next. Within weeks his syndicate held the leading position on the reef, Randfontein included.
entries.source_note: Meredith, Diamonds, Gold and War, ch. 18, drawing on Sauer, Ex Africa (1937).

entries.headline: Rhodes and Rudd hesitate
entries.digest: Rhodes and Rudd reached the Rand in the same month and bought part of Klein Paardekraal, setting up at Roodepoort. They turned down an option on 21 claims for £500 and claims at £40 each. Rhodes, burned by the Barberton crash, distrusted the conglomerate; Sauer was given a 15 per cent interest to buy for them.
entries.source_note: Meredith ch. 18; Phimister, 'Rhodes, Rhodesia and the Rand'.

entries.headline: A sworn statement: the reef is payable
entries.digest: Harrison put his experience on oath for the Mines Department: he had dug gold in Australia, he had prospected this reef, and in his judgement it was a payable goldfield. Two days later a petition signed by 73 men asked the government to proclaim the ground. The statement is the earliest dated claim of discovery.
entries.quote: long experience as an Australian gold digger
entries.source_note: Affidavit of 24 July 1886, quoted in City of Johannesburg, 'Three Georges strike paydirt'; SAHO timeline.

entries.headline: The government's inspectors report
entries.digest: Rissik and the Minister of Mines, C. J. Joubert, sent out early in August to judge whether the diggings should be proclaimed, reported on 12 August. They recommended a site for a village on Randjeslaagte, a triangle of unclaimed government land (uitvalgrond) left between farm boundaries. On 16 August a notice in the Staatscourant invited claims within a month.
entries.source_note: Heritage Portal, 'Naming Johannesburg' and 'Johannesburg goldfield discovered'.

entries.headline: The President signs the first proclamation
entries.digest: Kruger signed the proclamation declaring the first farms on the reef public diggings, placing them under the mining laws. In his memoirs he calls the discovery a complete revolution in the republic's finances. The page is displayed in Johannesburg as the city's birth certificate.
entries.quote: complete revolution in the financial aspect
entries.source_note: Heritage Portal, 'Johannesburg goldfield discovered' and 'When is Johannesburg's birthday?'; Memoirs (1902), ch. 9.

entries.headline: Nine o'clock: the proclamation read aloud
entries.digest: Von Brandis, the new Mining Commissioner, read the proclamation to the assembled diggers at nine in the morning; Driefontein and Elandsfontein were the first farms named, others followed weekly. Claims were to be leased, not sold, and pegging began. A statue of him reading it now stands in the city.
entries.source_note: City of Johannesburg, 'Three Georges strike paydirt' (time and date); Heritage Portal, 'When is Johannesburg's birthday?' (farms).

entries.headline: The first written use of the town's name
entries.digest: Von Brandis wrote to the State Secretary about the Surveyor-General's plan for the stands, under the name 'Johanensburg'. His letter does not say whom the name honoured. The original is missing; it survives only as a facsimile in a later history.
entries.source_note: Heritage Portal, 'Naming Johannesburg' (letter No. 4996/86).

entries.headline: Randjeslaagte and Langlaagte proclaimed
entries.digest: The triangle of Randjeslaagte and the discovery farm Langlaagte were proclaimed public diggings, and the next day a surveyor's tender to lay out the stands was accepted. This is the date the city now counts as its birthday. The government named the place Johannesburg, not Randjeslaagte, for reasons no record explains.
entries.source_note: Heritage Portal, 'When is Johannesburg's birthday?'; SAHO timeline.

entries.headline: Harrison claims the whole credit
entries.digest: Writing to the gold commissioner, Harrison described himself as the original prospector of a quarter of Gert Oosthuizen's farm and said that he and the owner had shown the quartz to the President in Pretoria, who declared it payable. Walker is not mentioned as co-finder. It is his last appearance in the record.
entries.source_note: Mining Weekly (2016); City of Johannesburg, 'Three Georges strike paydirt'.

entries.headline: Rhodes leaves on the night coach
entries.digest: A telegram reached Rhodes that his close friend Neville Pickering was dying in Kimberley. Rhodes left on the night coach, abandoning negotiations; Pickering died that morning, aged 29. Sauer was left on the Rand to carry on buying for the partnership.
entries.source_note: Meredith ch. 18, drawing on Sauer and FitzPatrick.

entries.headline: The discoverer sells out and disappears
entries.digest: About a month after the proclamation Harrison sold his Discoverer's Claim, reportedly for £10, and left the Rand. No later trace of him has been established. The claim on the main reef he had sworn was payable became part of one of the richest properties on earth.
entries.source_note: City of Johannesburg, 'Three Georges strike paydirt'; Heritage Portal (claim No. 19).

entries.headline: The first stands go under the hammer
entries.digest: The first sale of stands began and ran for three days, under 99-year leases at ten shillings a month. Stand No. 469 fetched £10 17s 6d; Thomas Beckett paid £1,005 for five stands in President Street; the total came to about £13,000. The surveyor had pegged 986 stands.
entries.source_note: Heritage Portal, 'Johannesburg goldfield discovered'; SAHO timeline.

entries.place: Main Reef properties, including the Ferreira
entries.headline: The American engineer's verdict
entries.digest: Gardner Williams spent ten days on the reef with Rhodes and Sauer and at the end told Sauer the properties were not worth the trouble, in a phrase Sauer never forgot. Rhodes, already doubtful, bought less than he could have. Williams went on to run De Beers.
entries.source_note: Mining Weekly, 'Rand goldfield: Not worth hell room' (2016), quoting Sauer, Ex Africa (1937).

entries.headline: Gold Fields of South Africa registered
entries.digest: Rhodes and Rudd's company, the Gold Fields of South Africa Ltd, was registered in London with a capital of £250,000. A 50-ton test crushing that winter at Luipaardsvlei had returned only 13 pennyweights a ton. The company would spend its first years looking north as much as down.
entries.source_note: Phimister, 'Rhodes, Rhodesia and the Rand' (exact day garbled in source).

entries.headline: The President hears the diggers' complaints
entries.digest: Kruger came to see the new town for himself, about four months after the proclamation. He was welcomed, then handed an address he says contained nothing but complaints against the government. He told the diggers the laws must be obeyed and referred grievances to the Diggers' Committee; looking back, he allowed he might have shown more consideration.
entries.quote: perhaps I should have been wiser
entries.source_note: Memoirs (1902), ch. 9; month from SAHO timeline and Meredith ch. 18.

entries.headline: A doctor for the mining camp
entries.digest: Sauer was appointed the town's first district surgeon. The camp was still a town of tents and corrugated iron; a Hospital Board followed in March 1888. He also chaired the Diggers' Committee that spoke to the government for the camp.
entries.source_note: Hans Sauer (Wikipedia).

entries.headline: The owners organise
entries.digest: The mining companies formed a chamber of mines in 1887 to speak to the government with one voice on claims, water, railways, the dynamite concession and labour. It was reconstituted in 1889 as the Witwatersrand Chamber of Mines with Eckstein as president.
entries.source_note: Minerals Council history; Hermann Eckstein (Wikipedia) gives 1889 for the reconstituted body.

entries.headline: The Eastern Star prints in the mining town
entries.digest: The Sheffield brothers' Eastern Star, sixteen years old in Grahamstown, published its first Johannesburg issue. The paper staked its future on the reef's future. In 1889 it took the name The Star.
entries.source_note: SAHO, 'The Star is published in Johannesburg'.

entries.headline: A second visit, and a special judge
entries.digest: Kruger visited Johannesburg again and found a friendlier crowd. He was asked to give the town a municipality; instead he appointed Dr Jorissen as a special judge for the goldfields. Self-government for the uitlander town remained withheld.
entries.source_note: Memoirs (1902), ch. 10.

entries.headline: Looking north for 'a big thing'
entries.digest: Rudd wrote to Alfred Curry that their best chance of a big thing now lay in a concession from the Ndebele king Lobengula, not on the Rand. Two months later, on 30 October 1888, the Rudd Concession was signed. Gold Fields shareholders heard of it in November.
entries.source_note: Phimister, 'Rhodes, Rhodesia and the Rand', citing Rudd to Curry, August 1888.

entries.headline: Arriving in the slump
entries.digest: Phillips came up from Kimberley to advise H. Eckstein & Co. as the boom broke. Below the oxidised surface the reef had turned to pyritic blue ore, from which mercury recovered too little gold; share prices collapsed and companies stopped milling. The Corner House began to buy the ground further south where the reef dipped, the future deep levels.
entries.source_note: Lionel Phillips (Wikipedia); Heritage Portal on the 1889 bust and the pyrites problem.

entries.headline: A chamber for a field in crisis
entries.digest: The Witwatersrand Chamber of Mines was reconstituted with Hermann Eckstein as president. Its first concerns were working costs: dynamite under a state concession, railway rates, water, and the price and supply of African labour. Its annual reports begin.
entries.source_note: Hermann Eckstein (Wikipedia); Levy (WCMAR series).

entries.headline: The republic's flag torn down
entries.digest: On a stop in Johannesburg on his way to meet the British High Commissioner, Kruger was met by a crowd; a riot broke out in front of Von Brandis's house and the republic's flag was pulled down. He told a deputation he had no contempt for the new population. The incident was raised in the House of Commons on 6 March as having happened the day before.
entries.quote: I have no contempt for the new population
entries.source_note: Memoirs (1902), ch. 10 (undated); Hansard HC Deb 6 March 1890, vol 342 c130.

entries.headline: Seven thousand men from the East Coast
entries.digest: The Chamber's report for 1890 recorded about 7,000 African workers drawn from the Portuguese territories on the East Coast, roughly half of the mines' African workforce, against about 4,000 from the northern Transvaal. The owners called this labour expensive, at about £3 a head to bring in. The men themselves left no record that has been found.
entries.source_note: WCMAR 1890 as analysed in Levy, 'The state, mineowners and labour regulation' (notes 8–17).

entries.headline: A combined wage cut, and a bid for the pass office
entries.digest: The companies agreed among themselves to cut the monthly wage of African underground workers sharply, and the Chamber asked the government to transfer the native pass and registration office to its own control. The Volksraad, protective of farmers' labour, refused; the Chamber set up its own Labour Commissioner. Men who deserted contracts could be prosecuted under the Master and Servant law of 1880.
entries.source_note: Levy, citing WCMAR 1890, pp. 66–69; wage figures in the source are garbled and are not given here.

entries.headline: Cyanide tried at the Salisbury
entries.digest: A pilot plant at the Salisbury mine tested the MacArthur-Forrest cyanide process, patented in Glasgow, on reef, concentrates and tailings, recovering about nine-tenths of the gold against perhaps seven-tenths by mercury. For the owners and their deep-level plans, it was the turning point. About a third of the town's people had left during the slump.
entries.source_note: Heritage Portal (node 1421); SAHO timeline gives May 1890 for the introduction. The Chamber's own report on the trial was not consulted directly.

entries.headline: Gold Fields turns its back on the Rand
entries.digest: Rudd stated that Gold Fields would concentrate its forces in Mashonaland rather than on the Witwatersrand. The company made about £16,000 in 1891 and paid no dividend. It would come back to the Rand through the deep levels a year later.
entries.source_note: Phimister, 'Rhodes, Rhodesia and the Rand'.

entries.headline: A manufacturing town without the smoke
entries.digest: Arriving after four days by coach, Churchill found Johannesburg very English in appearance, like a factory town without the noise and dirt, and full of promise, but with unpaved dusty streets, no lighting and few police. He put the field's output at 60,000 ounces a month. Share values, he said, had swollen to nearly forty millions and shrunk to four.
entries.source_note: Men, Mines and Animals in South Africa, ch. IV (1895 ed.).

entries.headline: Nine hundred African men and a cyanide trial
entries.digest: At the Robinson mine Churchill was told of 130 Europeans and about 900 African workers, five miles of workings and a shaft 500 feet deep. Cyanide was being tried on the tailings and chlorination on concentrates; it was too early, he wrote, to judge. He recorded white carpenters' and mechanics' weekly wages but not what the African workers were paid.
entries.quote: one of the finest gold mines in the world
entries.source_note: Men, Mines and Animals, ch. V.

entries.headline: A private letter about Beit
entries.digest: Writing privately to his wife, Churchill described a visit to silver mines, his strained dealings with his syndicate partners, his opinion of Alfred Beit and his plans to go north. The public letters praised the Randlords' enterprise; the private one weighed them as partners.
entries.source_note: Churchill Archives Centre catalogue, letter of 17 June 1891.

entries.headline: Kruger between sittings, with his pipe
entries.digest: Churchill met Kruger during an adjournment of the Second Volksraad: a tall, stout man of about 65 with a grave, shrewd but not unkindly face, smoking a short pipe hastily. Kruger said a Boer trek into Mashonaland would cause no trouble. Churchill's letters condemned the republic's taxation and its treatment of Africans in the same pages.
entries.quote: a grave, shrewd, but by no means unkindly countenance
entries.source_note: Men, Mines and Animals, ch. VI; party left Pretoria Friday 3 July 1891.

entries.headline: Succeeding Eckstein at the Chamber
entries.digest: Phillips succeeded Hermann Eckstein as president of the Chamber of Mines. The cyanide process was by then general, the first train from the Cape arrived on 14 September 1892, and the deep levels were being floated. Labour supply and the dynamite monopoly headed the Chamber's complaints to Pretoria.
entries.source_note: Lionel Phillips (Wikipedia); SAHO timeline (railway).

entries.headline: Mashonaland 'discredited'; the merger
entries.digest: Rudd conceded to Curry that the company's whole Mashonaland holding was discredited. In August Gold Fields amalgamated with three smaller firms as Consolidated Gold Fields of South Africa, capital £1,250,000, and took a share in Beit's Rand Mines deep-level venture.
entries.source_note: Phimister, 'Rhodes, Rhodesia and the Rand'.

entries.headline: New pass regulations for the mines
entries.digest: The Star reported pass regulations for African mineworkers, drafted by the Chamber in 1894 under the Gold Law and promulgated about eighteen months later. They tightened the owners' control over where African workers could go and whom they could leave, backed by the Master and Servant law. Eight days later Jameson's force crossed the border.
entries.source_note: The Star, 21 December 1895, cited by Levy, note 20; SAHO timeline (29 December 1895).

entries.headline: The Reform leaders surrender
entries.digest: After the failure of the Jameson Raid at Doornkop, Phillips and the other Reform Committee leaders surrendered to the republic and later pleaded guilty. The ringleaders were sentenced to death, reprieved and fined £25,000 each.
entries.source_note: Lionel Phillips (Wikipedia).

entries.headline: Rissik: the town was named for Joubert and me
entries.digest: Ten years on, in a departmental note, Rissik wrote that Johannesburg had been named after himself and Christiaan Johannes Joubert, both Johannes. It is the only written statement on the name from anyone involved. Others credited Kruger, also a Johannes, or the mining official Johannes Meyer.
entries.source_note: Heritage Portal, 'Naming Johannesburg' (note quoted by M. S. Appelgryn, Die Vaderland, 1971).

entries.headline: The President remembers the gold
entries.digest: In memoirs dictated in exile after the war, Kruger set down General Piet Joubert's warning to a burgher who brought news of a new reef: this gold would soak the country in blood. He held that the franchise grievance had been worked up by intriguers and that Britain would not have lifted a finger for the uitlanders but for the gold.
entries.quote: this gold will cause our country to be soaked in blood
entries.source_note: Memoirs (1902), ch. 9.

entries.headline: The Strubens' claim to have opened the Rand
entries.digest: Five years after Harry Struben's death, his Recollections appeared, edited by his daughter Edith. They present the Confidence Reef, the Volksraad appeal and the battery as the opening of the Witwatersrand. A monument to the brothers was later raised and has since been destroyed.
entries.source_note: Harry Struben (Wikipedia); Heritage Portal, 'Struben Monument destroyed but not forgotten'.

entries.headline: Walker's account, thirty-eight years on
entries.digest: The Sunday Times published Walker's account of finding the outcrop and panning it in Mrs Oosthuizen's frying pan. He was 71, living on a small allowance from the Chamber of Mines. He died in Krugersdorp on 18 September that year. A government inquiry opened in the late 1930s; its report, in 1941, did not settle who found the reef.
entries.source_note: Mining Weekly (2016); Wigan Local History (death); City of Johannesburg (1941 report).

convergences.label: The week of the find on Langlaagte, February 1886
convergences.note: Three men claim the same week and none of them wrote at the time. Walker remembers a frying pan, Honeyball a Sunday and a second outcrop, and Harrison's sworn statements of July and October name only himself. The Strubens' battery and cottage work is what brought them all to the ridge.

convergences.label: Late July 1886: the affidavit and the buyers
convergences.note: In the same days that Harrison swore the reef was payable and 73 diggers petitioned for proclamation, Robinson was buying Langlaagte with Beit's money and Rhodes and Rudd were turning down options. The prospector's oath and the capitalists' purchases are different readings of the same rock.

convergences.label: Proclamation, September 1886
convergences.note: The inspectors' report, the President's signature and the commissioner's reading on the veld are three steps of one act of state. Kruger remembered it as financial salvation, and Von Brandis's job was to turn it into leases and fees.

convergences.label: October 1886: a name, a town, a vanishing
convergences.note: As Randjeslaagte was proclaimed and first written as 'Johanensburg', Harrison made his last statement and sold out, and Rhodes left on the night coach. Rissik's claim about the name came ten years later.

convergences.label: February 1887: the President's visit and the London flotation
convergences.note: Kruger was hearing diggers' complaints in a tent town while Gold Fields was being registered in London on the strength of ground Rhodes half doubted. Sauer had just heard Williams call the reef worthless.

convergences.label: 1890: the flag, the wage cut and the cyanide
convergences.note: In one year the uitlander crowd pulled down the republic's flag, the owners combined to cut African wages and sought control of the pass office, and the Salisbury trial showed that cyanide could save the field. Kruger saw disloyalty, and the Chamber saw working costs.

convergences.label: June 1891: a London visitor's month on the Rand
convergences.note: Churchill counted the Robinson's 900 African workers and praised its management while Rudd's Gold Fields was turning away to Mashonaland. In Pretoria he met the President whose government his letters attacked.

convergences.label: Remembering the find: memoirs of the 1920s
convergences.note: Struben's Recollections (1920), Walker's newspaper account and Phillips's Some Reminiscences (both 1924) all appeared within four years. The prospectors were claiming the discovery and the Randlord was explaining himself.

Honeyball's recollection places Walker at the Oosthuizen house with the first rock sample.
Walker built a cottage for the Strubens and worked on their Wilgespruit battery in early 1886.
Kruger thanked the Struben brothers in the Volksraad on 5 June 1885.
Brothers and partners in the Confidence Reef.
Von Brandis was Kruger's Mining Commissioner; the 1890 riot took place outside his house during the President's visit.
Rissik credited himself and Joubert with the name; Kruger, asked, remarked only that he too was a Johannes.
Sauer bought claims on the Rand for Rhodes and Rudd on a 15 per cent share.
Churchill interviewed Kruger in Pretoria in June 1891 and described him in Men, Mines and Animals.
Phillips joined Eckstein's firm in 1889 and succeeded him as Chamber president in 1892.
The Star printed the pass regulations the Chamber had drafted; the Chamber's reports were reviewed in its columns.
As a Reform Committee leader Phillips was tried and sentenced by Kruger's republic in 1896.
Churchill's letters repeat the owners' figures and complaints about taxation and the dynamite monopoly.

threads_out.note: The Rand's capital, its first magnates (Rhodes, Beit, Robinson, Phillips, Eckstein's partners) and its closed-compound model of African labour came straight from the Kimberley diamond fields.
Harrison swore his judgement on the strength of the Australian goldfields, themselves opened by men back from California; the Rand's diggers and engineers carried methods and law from those rushes.
The Klondike strike came as the Rand turned from diggings to deep-level corporate mining; the two fields fed the gold supply that ended the 1890s price deflation.

The Premier mine that produced the Cullinan lay near Pretoria in the same Transvaal, whose post-war government gave the stone to Edward VII in 1907, the same decade the Rand imported Chinese indentured miners.
From the 1890s South Africa became the world's largest gold producer; Rand output underpinned the gold standard and later the sterling and Bretton Woods arrangements that ended in 1971.
